newsitem.title: USA: White House faces showdown on documents.
newsitem.headline: White House faces showdown on documents.

text.p: Congress and the Clinton administration faced a new legal showdown Tuesday with the White House undecided on whether to defy a congressional committee investigating campaign fund raising.

The immediate decision facing the White House was whether President Clinton's legal counsel Charles Ruff should comply with a request to testify Thursday before a House committee investigating fund raising.
A White House official said a decision would be made within a day.

Indiana Representative Dan Burton, the Republican chairman of the House government reform and oversight committee, called the hearing to ask Ruff why the White House refused to comply with subpoenas of documents relating to possible illegal campaign contributions by foreigners.
"The issue to be resolved is whether this is just an exercise to get some TV exposure or a genuine effort to produce a result that would be acceptable to both sides," the White House official said.

Thursday's hearing loomed as the next flashpoint in a growing confrontation between congressional Republicans and the White House. If Ruff declines to appear or refuses to hand over the documents, the House committee could vote on a "contempt of Congress" resolution as early as Friday and send it to the full House next week.
In a letter to Ruff last Friday, Burton said the White House had been stonewalling the committee for months.
"Given the White House response to date, I have concluded ... that I have no alternative but to hold a hearing to consider your refusal to fully respond to the committee's subpoenas," Burton wrote.
"I am formally requesting that you attend to explain why you should not be held in contempt of Congress," he added.

The White House has said it would allow Burton and his investigators to look at the documents it wants to see but not to copy them and remove them from the White House because of the danger they would be leaked to the media.

Representative Henry Waxman, the ranking Democrat on the committee, said his staff had seen the documents and "there's nothing particularly in those documents that's going to inform us in any particular way."
Waxman accused Burton of "grandstanding" by trying to portray himself as a man fighting against the power of the White House.
Some of the documents relate to former Associate Attorney General Webster Hubbell, who was recently released after serving a jail sentence for defrauding his Arkansas law firm.
In the period between resigning from the Justice Department and beginning his sentence, Hubbell received more than $500,000 from various individuals and companies for work as a legal consultant.
Burton and other Republicans suspect it was hush money to prevent him testifying about what he knew. Hubbell has indicated he will invoke the Fifth Amendment and refuse to testify further.
In an interview Sunday, Burton said it was "pretty evident" to him that the president and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton knew about the money paid to Hubbell.
Other documents demanded by the committee related to the activities of Asian-Americans and Asian business interests, including former Democratic fund-raiser John Huang.
